slides.text:
A binary tree is a linked list where every node has two pointers: a left child and a right child. You will build trees by hand, walk them in different orders, grow and search a sorted tree, measure it, flip it and remove nodes from it.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
node:
    value
    left  -> a node, or nil
    right -> a node, or nil

slides.text:
A tree is either empty (`nil`) or a node with a left tree and a right tree. So a function over a tree always has the same shape: stop at `nil`, then deal with the node and with each side.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
visit(node):
    if node is nil:
        stop
    visit(left of node)
    visit(right of node)

slides.text: Where the work sits decides the order a tree is walked in: before the two calls, between them, or after them. Each order has its own use.

exercises.title: A node with two children
exercises.guide: Build a tiny tree by hand: a root with a left and a right child.

chunks.guide: Like a list node, but with two pointers: one for each child. A `nil` pointer means no child there.

notes.text: Points at the left child, or is nil.

chunks.guide: The root is a pointer to a node. Hang two new nodes from it.

notes.text: Links a new node as the left child.

chunks.guide: Follow the pointers down. The child of a child does not exist yet, so it is nil.
chunks.text:
fmt.Println(root.Value)
    fmt.Println(root.Left.Value, root.Right.Value)
    fmt.Println(root.Left.Left == nil)

exercises.title: Count the nodes
exercises.guide: Count every node of a tree with a function that calls itself.

chunks.guide: An empty tree has no nodes. Otherwise count this node, plus everything on each side.

notes.text: An empty tree: nothing left to count.
The left child is itself a smaller tree.

chunks.guide: Nested literals build the whole tree: each child sits inside its parent.

notes.text: A child can be written inside its parent.

chunks.guide: `nil` is an empty tree, so its count is 0.
chunks.text: fmt.Println(count(root), count(nil))

exercises.title: Add up the values
exercises.guide: Fill the gaps so the function adds up every value in the tree.

exercises.title: Left, node, right
exercises.guide: Print a tree by visiting the left side, then the node, then the right side.

chunks.guide: The print sits between the two calls: the left side is finished before this node, the right side comes after.

notes.text: Runs only after the whole left side is done.

chunks.guide: The tree is already built in the file. Walk it from the root.
chunks.text: inorder(root)

exercises.title: Print before the calls
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output. The tree has 4 at the root, 2 and 5 below it, and 1 and 3 below the 2.
exercises.explanation: The node is printed before its sides, so a parent comes before its children: 4, then the whole left side (2, 1, 3), then 5.

exercises.title: Children before parents
exercises.guide: Print a tree so every node comes after both of its sides.

chunks.guide: Same walk as before, with the print moved after both calls.

notes.text: Both sides are done before this node prints.

chunks.guide: The root is the last one to print.
chunks.text: postorder(root)

slides.text:
In a search tree, everything on the left of a node is smaller and everything on the right is larger, for every node. A search can drop a whole side at each step.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
search(node, value):
    if value < node's value:
        look only on the left
    otherwise:
        look only on the right

slides.text: Inserting follows the path a search would take and puts the new node where the search ends: at an empty (`nil`) spot. The same values in another order build a different tree.

exercises.title: Insert into a search tree
exercises.guide: Put each new value where a search for it would end.

chunks.guide: Smaller values go left, the others go right. At an empty spot, the new node is created and returned.

notes.text: An empty spot: the new value becomes a leaf.
Stores the returned node back as the left child.

chunks.guide: Start from an empty tree and insert the values one by one.

notes.text: A nil pointer is an empty tree.

chunks.guide: See where each value landed.
chunks.text:
l := root.Left
    fmt.Println(root.Value)
    fmt.Println(l.Value, root.Right.Value)
    fmt.Println(l.Left.Value, l.Right.Value)

exercises.title: Where did the values land?
exercises.guide: `insert` is the function you typed. Each value prints on its own line; the options list them in order.
exercises.code:
var root *Node
for _, v := range []int{5, 3, 8, 4} {
    root = insert(root, v)
}
fmt.Println(root.Left.Value)
fmt.Println(root.Left.Right.Value)
fmt.Println(root.Right.Value)
exercises.explanation: 5 is the root. 3 goes left of it and 8 goes right. 4 is smaller than 5, so it goes left, then larger than 3, so it goes right of 3.

exercises.title: Complete the insert
exercises.guide: Fill the gaps so smaller values go left and the function returns the node it received.

exercises.title: Search for a value
exercises.guide: Find out if a value is in the tree, going down only one side.

chunks.guide: A match ends the search. Otherwise only one side can hold the value. Reaching nil means it is not there.

notes.text: The right side is skipped: it holds only larger values.

chunks.guide: The tree is built in the file. Look for a value that is there and one that is not.
chunks.text:
fmt.Println(contains(root, 3))
    fmt.Println(contains(root, 7))

exercises.title: Search with a loop
exercises.guide: The same search, walking down with a loop instead of calls.

chunks.guide: Move the pointer down one level each turn, until a match or a nil.

notes.text: Moves this copy of the pointer; the tree is untouched.

chunks.guide: Try a value that is there and one that is not.
chunks.text:
fmt.Println(contains(root, 1))
    fmt.Println(contains(root, 6))

exercises.title: Smallest and largest
exercises.guide: Find the extremes of a search tree without looking at every node.

chunks.guide: The smallest value is at the far left: keep going left while there is a left child.

notes.text: Stops on the last node, so the tree can't be empty.

chunks.guide: The mirror image: the largest value is at the far right.
The tree is built in the file.
chunks.text: fmt.Println(smallest(root), largest(root))

slides.text: The shape of a search tree depends on the order of insertion. Values that arrive sorted make a chain, and a search then visits every node, like in a list. The **height** shows how tall the tree got.

Changing a tree means changing pointers. A function that may replace the node it receives returns the new subtree, and the caller stores it back, as in `n.Left = f(n.Left)`. Flipping a tree this way breaks its ordering, so it stops being a search tree.

Removing a node has three cases, depending on its children.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
remove(node):
    no left child:
        use the right child
    no right child:
        use the left child
    both children:
        copy in the next larger value
        remove that value from the right

exercises.title: How tall is the tree
exercises.guide: Measure a tree, and see what the order of insertion does to it.

chunks.guide: An empty tree has height 0. Otherwise it is one more than its taller side.

notes.text: Measure each side first, then compare.

chunks.guide: Seven values, starting from the middle one.
The same seven values, but in order.
Same values, different shapes.
chunks.text: fmt.Println(height(balanced), height(chain))

exercises.title: Complete the height
exercises.guide: Fill the gaps so the function returns one more than its taller side.

exercises.title: Values in order
exercises.guide: `inorder` prints each value on its own line, and the options list them in order.
exercises.explanation: In a search tree everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is larger. Walking left, node, right visits the values from smallest to largest.

exercises.title: Flip a tree
exercises.guide: Swap the children of every node, so the tree becomes its mirror.

chunks.guide: Swap the two pointers of a node, then do the same in both children. The tree changes in place.

notes.text: Swaps the pointers; each child brings its subtree.

chunks.guide: Check the children before the flip.
chunks.text: fmt.Println(root.Left.Value, root.Right.Value)

chunks.guide: Flip it and look again. The 2 is now on the right.
chunks.text:
mirror(root)
    fmt.Println(root.Left.Value, root.Right.Value)
    fmt.Println(root.Right.Left.Value)

exercises.title: Remove a node
exercises.guide: Remove a leaf, or a node with one child. Two children come next.

chunks.guide: `remove` returns the new root of the tree it was given.
chunks.text:
func remove(n *Node, v int) *Node {
}

chunks.guide: Walk down like insert. Each step stores the result back and returns the node.
Found it. With one child or none, hand back the child: the parent links to it and the node is gone.

notes.text: The parent will point at this child instead.

chunks.guide: Remove a leaf, then a node with one child.

notes.text: Store the result: the root itself could be removed.

chunks.text:
root = remove(root, 2)
    root = remove(root, 8)

chunks.guide: The 2 is gone, and the 8 was replaced by its child.
chunks.text:
fmt.Println(root.Left.Left == nil)
    fmt.Println(root.Right.Value)

exercises.title: Remove with two children
exercises.guide: Handle the last case: a node that has both children.

chunks.guide: The earlier cases are in the file. With two children, take the smallest value of the right side, put it in this node, then remove it from there.

notes.text: The next larger value in the tree.
The node stays; only its value is replaced.

chunks.guide: Remove the root, which has two children.
chunks.text: root = remove(root, 5)

chunks.guide: The 7 moved up, and its old place is empty.
chunks.text:
fmt.Println(root.Value, root.Left.Value)
    fmt.Println(root.Right.Value)
    fmt.Println(root.Right.Left == nil)
